en: The Sūtra on King Māndhātṛ, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. It was thus.
At that time, Ānanda reflected in a secluded place:
"In this world, those who feel even a slight degree of weariness toward the five objects of desire are few; many remain until death without ever knowing contentment."
After midday, Ānanda went before the Buddha, prostrated himself, and then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"While reflecting in seclusion, I thought that among the people of the world, those who feel even a slight degree of weariness toward the five objects of desire are few, while those who do not know contentment until death are many."

The Buddha said, “It is exactly as Ānanda has said: among the people of the world, those who feel even a slight degree of weariness toward the five objects of desire are few, while those who remain ignorant of satiety until death are many.”

Why is this so? Formerly there was a king named Mandhātṛ; he was born from the crown of his mother’s head, and for that reason he was named Mandhātṛ. Later, he became a Cakravartin king, and the regions of the east, west, south, and north all came under his dominion.

There are seven treasures: first, the golden wheel; second, the white elephant; third, the dark-blue horse; fourth, the bright moon pearl; fifth, the jade-like woman; sixth, the holy minister; and seventh, the commander-in-chief who guides the way. Thus does a Cakravartin King possess these seven treasures.
King Jen-hsien cultivated the True Dharma and did not trouble the myriad people.
He had a thousand sons, all of whom were handsome and highly talented, robust and powerful; the four quarters of the world were all brought under his submission.
Having reigned for several thousand years, he thought to himself:
"I possess the four continents; the population is flourishing, grain is cheap and abundant, and the people are mostly wealthy."
The king further thought to himself:

"I have a thousand sons, all handsome beyond compare, of extraordinary talent, and possessed of fierce strength and vigor. It would be wonderful if Heaven were to rain down coins of gold and silver for me for seven days and seven nights."
Upon hearing these words, the deva granted his wish and immediately rained down coins, gold, and silver for seven days and seven nights.
Seeing the rain of coins, gold, and silver for seven days and seven nights, the king was filled with great joy, and they enjoyed themselves together for several thousand years.
The king thought to himself:

"The four continents all belong to me; I have a thousand sons and the seven treasures are all before me. Whatever I desired to obtain, I have already obtained it. Furthermore, Heaven has not thwarted my wishes, raining down coins, gold, and silver for seven days and seven nights."

When King Mandhātṛ heard that in the south there was the land of Jambudvīpa, where the people were exceedingly joyful and flourishing, he desired to go there. As soon as this thought arose, he took up his seven treasures and the fourfold army, and they all flew together to that place.

Jambudvīpa is twenty-eight thousand li in extent; when the king appears in that land, it immediately submits and becomes his domain. Because the king performed good deeds in his past lives, he has attained such blessings as these.
Having lived for several thousand years in the country of Aparagoyānī, the king again conceived this thought:

"I possess a great kingdom in the western direction called Aparagoyānī, thirty-two hundred thousand *li* in length and breadth; I possess the seven treasures; the heavens rained down coins, gold, and silver for me for seven days and seven nights; I have a thousand sons, all of whom are peerlessly handsome, highly talented, courageous, fierce, and strong; and I possess the southern continent of Jambudvīpa, two hundred and eighty thousand *li* in extent."
The king heard that in the east there was a kingdom called Pūrvavideha, where the population was flourishing, grain was cheap and abundant, and the country was greatly prosperous.

The king desired to go there; as soon as the thought arose, he took his seven treasures and the fourfold army and flew there together. The king of that land and its people then submitted and became his subjects, and the king consequently ruled the country with the True Dharma.
After many thousands of years had passed in this manner, the king again conceived this thought:
"I possess the kingdom of Jambudvīpa, twenty-eight thousand li; I possess the kingdom of Aparagoyānī, thirty-two thousand li; and I possess the kingdom of Pūrvavideha, thirty-six thousand li."
When the king heard that in the north there was Uttarakuru, where the world is greatly joyful and the population is flourishing, he desired to go to that country.
In that land, there is no poverty; there is no distinction between the noble and the lowly, nor between the strong and the weak; there are no slaves or masters, for all are equal.
"May my people, retinues, and officials all partake together of this naturally produced non-glutinous rice, naturally produced clothing, garments, ornaments, and various precious jewels.
As soon as the king conceived this thought, he took up the seven treasures and the fourfold army, and they all flew together into the realm of Uttarakuru.
Seeing from afar that the ground was a brilliant green like the color of emerald feathers, the king asked his ministers,
"Do you all see this ground, which is a brilliant green like the color of emerald feathers?"
The border official replied,
"Indeed, I have seen it. The king said:
"Therefore, this is the continent of Uttarakuru.
As the king proceeded further, he again saw the ground perfectly white like snow. The king spoke again to his ministers, saying:
"Do you see this ground that is perfectly white?"
The border official replied,
"Indeed, I have seen it. The king said:
"Therefore, on the continent of Uttarakuru, rice is naturally produced and pounded; you all should eat it together.
Just as he was proceeding further, he saw from afar various jewel-trees and trees bearing a hundred kinds of garments, with gold, silver, jade rings, and necklaces all hanging from them.
The King asked his ministers, "Do you all see these various jewel-trees?"
The border official replied,
“Indeed, I have seen it. The king said:
"Therefore, there are trees of a hundred kinds of garments, as well as trees of gold, silver, jade rings, and necklaces; you all must go together and take them to wear.
The king then proceeded forward to the land of Uttarakuru, and the people there all submitted and became his subjects.
The King ruled over Uttarakuru for several thousand years, after which a thought arose in his mind, and he reflected:
"I possess the land of Jambudvīpa, the land of Aparagoyānī, the land of Pūrvavideha, and the land of Uttarakuru, forty thousand *li* in extent."
The king desired to ascend Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains composed of the four jewels, to reach the abode of Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

As soon as the king formed this thought, he and his seven treasures along with his hundred officials were all transported by flight to the summit of Mount Sumeru, where they proceeded to enter the palace of Śakra, the Heavenly King.
Seeing King Mandhātṛ approaching from afar, Śakra rose to greet him and said,
"I have often heard of your virtues and have long desired to meet you.
It is most auspicious that you have come, O Benevolent One!"
He then took him by the hand and sat with him, offering half of his seat to King Mandhātṛ.

As soon as they were seated, he looked up toward the heavens and saw celestial maidens in attendance; their palaces were all constructed from the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, amber, and musaragalva.
Upon seeing this, he thought to himself:
"I possess Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru; in my house there is a rain of gold and silver for seven days and seven nights."
King Mandhātṛ thought to himself:
"If the Heavenly King Śakra were to die, I would wish to take his place and rule over the heavens, just as it was pleasurable for me when I ruled the world below."
As soon as the King conceived this thought, the spirit departed; it immediately returned to the world below, and the King was struck by illness, becoming so weak that he was confined to his bed.
All the ministers and officials in the King's retinue gathered by the King’s bedside and asked him:
"Is there perhaps some final testament you wish to leave behind?"
The king said: "Let those among you who dare ask me:
'What kind of final testament does the king have?'"
"You should say to him:

'When the king was alive, he ruled over the four continents; the heavens rained down coins of gold and silver for seven days and seven nights; the king had a thousand sons and possessed the seven treasures, all of whom were able to fly.'"

When the king ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Śakra, the King of Devas, rose to welcome him, honored him with gifts, and inquired after his well-being; he then offered him half of his own seat, yet the king still conceived the desire to obtain the position of Śakra, the King of Devas.
As soon as he gave rise to this thought, he immediately fell down upon the ground, afflicted by illness and weakness.
He repented, saying:
"People never reach satiety until death; those who know contentment are few indeed."

The Sūtra says: "One is not satisfied merely by having rain of money, gold, and silver for seven days and seven nights; its benefit is slight, while its fault is great and heavy. A person of wisdom should reflect upon this matter."

Furthermore, even obtaining the status of Śakra, King of Devas, would not suffice; it is only when a person practices the Way and attains the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, or Pratyekabuddha, up until the attainment of the Buddha-way, that they finally reach fulfillment.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"The King Mandhātṛ at that time was my own self.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, Ānanda rejoiced and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra on King Mandhātu Spoken by the Buddha
